subject: Medicine
summary: Nutrition is a cornerstone of health, influencing disease risk, recovery and mortality. In low‑resource East African hospitals clinicians must assess, diagnose and manage malnutrition with limited investigations.

sections.p: Nutrition refers to the intake, absorption and utilization of nutrients required for growth, maintenance and repair. Clinical malnutrition is diagnosed when anthropometry or clinical signs indicate inadequate nutrient stores.
b: BMI <18.5 kg/m² in adults
Mid‑upper arm circumference (MUAC) <23 cm (women) or <22 cm (men)
Weight loss >10 % in 3–6 months

sections.p: The WHO/UNICEF Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) classification is used for adults and children.
b: Moderate acute malnutrition: BMI 16–16.9 kg/m² or MUAC 21–22.9 cm
Severe acute malnutrition: BMI <16 kg/m² or MUAC <21 cm
Chronic malnutrition: stunting (height‑for‑age <‑2 SD) in children

sections.p: In East Africa, the most common drivers are socioeconomic, infectious and chronic disease related.
b: Food insecurity and poverty
Chronic infections: HIV, TB, malaria, schistosomiasis
Gastrointestinal losses: chronic diarrhoea, parasitic infections
Malabsorption: celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency
Increased metabolic demand: severe burns, trauma, surgery
Medication effects: antiretrovirals, anti‑TB drugs causing nausea

sections.p: Patients may appear thin, have loss of subcutaneous fat, muscle wasting, edema, or skin changes.
b: Visible loss of muscle bulk (temples, clavicles)
Dry, thin hair and brittle nails
Koilonychia (spoon nails)
Peripheral edema in severe protein deficiency
Fatigue, poor wound healing, recurrent infections

t.b: Is the patient underweight? – Confirms chronic energy deficiency
Is there acute malnutrition? – Quick bedside screen when scales unavailable
Is there protein‑energy deficiency? – Low <30 g/L suggests severe malnutrition but may be affected by inflammation
Is there anemia or infection? – Microcytic anemia points to iron deficiency; leukocytosis may indicate infection
Which vitamins/minerals are deficient? – Low ferritin, vitamin D, B12 guide supplementation
Is there parasitic loss? – Positive result directs anti‑helminth therapy

sections.p: Severe malnutrition can rapidly become life‑threatening.
b: Refeeding syndrome (electrolyte shifts on nutrition re‑initiation)
Severe edema or ascites indicating hypoalbuminemia
Impaired immunity leading to sepsis
Cardiac failure from thiamine deficiency (wet beriberi)
Delayed wound healing and pressure sores

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then provide safe nutritional rehabilitation.
b: Treat infections first (e.g., start anti‑TB therapy, antiretrovirals).
Correct electrolyte abnormalities before feeding (especially potassium, phosphate, magnesium).
Start low‑energy, high‑protein oral therapeutic foods (e.g., Plumpy’Nut, locally prepared millet‑based porridge).
If oral intake impossible, use nasogastric feeding with 10‑15 kcal/kg/day, advancing slowly.
Avoid high‑dose glucose solutions alone to prevent refeeding hypophosphatemia.

sections.p: Nutrition status must be monitored regularly and underlying risk factors addressed.
b: Weekly weight and MUAC checks during refeeding.
Educate caregivers on balanced diets using locally available foods.
Screen for HIV, TB and parasitic infections annually.
Promote food‑security programmes and agricultural support.
Vaccinate against measles, pneumococcus and influenza to reduce infection‑related wasting.
Hyperthyroidism – weight loss with tremor and tachycardia, not loss of fat stores.
Chronic heart failure – cachexia but accompanied by peripheral edema and raised JVP.
Depression – reduced intake but usually without physical signs of muscle wasting.
Serum albumin falls in inflammation; a normal level does not exclude malnutrition.
BMI may be misleading in oedematous patients; use MUAC instead.
Micronutrient assays often unavailable; clinical signs guide empiric supplementation.

whenToSeekHelp: Altered mental status after starting feeds (suspect refeeding syndrome)
Unexplained fever or sepsis in a malnourished patient

faq.q: Can a patient with normal BMI still be malnourished?
faq.a: Yes; edema or high muscle mass can mask low fat stores, so MUAC and clinical signs are essential.
Rapid carbohydrate intake drives insulin, causing phosphate, potassium and magnesium shifts that can precipitate cardiac arrest.

faq.q: What is the first step if a laboratory test is unavailable?
faq.a: Rely on bedside anthropometry (BMI, MUAC) and clinical signs to guide immediate management.

exam: What bedside measurements would you use to screen for acute malnutrition in a 3‑year‑old child when scales are unavailable? — MUAC; <12.5 cm indicates moderate, <11.5 cm severe.

A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with BMI 15 kg/m² and peripheral edema. What is your immediate management priority? — Correct electrolytes and start low‑calorie feeding to avoid refeeding syndrome before aggressive caloric increase.
How does chronic malaria contribute to malnutrition, and what investigations would you order? — Repeated haemolysis and appetite loss; order malaria smear, full blood count and stool for parasites.

Explain why serum albumin is not a reliable sole marker of nutritional status in an acutely ill patient. — It falls with inflammation and fluid shifts, giving a false impression of protein deficiency.
When would you choose nasogastric feeding over oral therapeutic foods in a malnourished patient? — When the patient cannot protect the airway, has severe oral lesions, or is unconscious.
Identify two micronutrients most commonly deficient in East African malnutrition and their clinical signs. — Iron (microcytic anemia, fatigue) and vitamin A (night blindness, xerophthalmia).
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for a malnourished child with suspected refeeding syndrome? — New onset cardiac arrhythmia or severe weakness with hypophosphatemia.
Distinguish between protein‑energy malnutrition and wet beriberi in an alcoholic patient. — Both have edema, but wet beriberi shows high-output cardiac failure and responds to thiamine.
